assessment.nobel_worthiness: A foundational and unusually broad political-economy research program connecting political institutions, accountability, state capacity, and fiscal choices to economic outcomes.
assessment.attribution: Besley, Persson, and Tabellini are central and complementary architects of the listed contribution, spanning theory, empirics, and institutional application.
assessment.maturity: The core work has shaped political economy for decades and has generated a mature empirical research agenda.
uncertainties: The contribution combines several linked strands, making a single sharply bounded prize citation challenging.
Causal attribution from institutions to economic outcomes remains empirically demanding.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The heterogeneous-firm framework fundamentally changed the analysis of trade, productivity, selection, and aggregate gains from openness.
assessment.attribution: Melitz supplied the defining framework, while Helpman and Redding made central theoretical and empirical contributions to its development and use.
assessment.maturity: The framework is deeply embedded in modern trade research and has extensive empirical confirmation.
uncertainties: Credit is difficult to delimit because firm heterogeneity developed through a large connected trade literature.
The balance between foundational modeling and later empirical extensions requires careful citation design.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Population-scale administrative-data research has transformed measurement of intergenerational mobility and made local opportunity a central economic and policy question.
assessment.attribution: Chetty and Hendren are especially central to the mobility program; Friedman is an important collaborator in the broader administrative-data research agenda.
assessment.maturity: The findings are influential, replicated across settings, and already reshape research and policy debate.
uncertainties: The work is comparatively recent for a prize and its long-run interpretation remains under active study.
Many collaborators contributed to the wider research program.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Their work provided durable economic foundations for treating natural capital, biodiversity, and exhaustible resources as central components of social wealth and sustainability.
assessment.attribution: Dasgupta and Heal are both closely associated with the conceptual development of the listed environmental-economics contribution.
assessment.maturity: The research has had a long intellectual life and growing relevance as environmental constraints become quantitatively central.
uncertainties: The policy measurement of biodiversity and inclusive wealth remains methodologically unsettled.
The contribution overlaps with a broad environmental-economics tradition.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The misallocation framework gave a powerful, portable account of how distorted allocation across firms can explain productivity and income differences.
assessment.attribution: Hsieh and Klenow are central to the seminal quantitative formulation; Restuccia made major related contributions to the broader program.
assessment.maturity: The approach has become a standard tool in growth and development and has stimulated a substantial follow-on literature.
uncertainties: Measured wedges can reflect forces other than inefficient distortions.
Quantitative welfare implications depend on strong modeling and data assumptions.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The program on fairness, reciprocity, and inequity aversion changed economic models of behavior and linked laboratory evidence to contracts, organizations, and markets.
assessment.attribution: Fehr, Falk, and Schmidt made distinctive and mutually reinforcing experimental and theoretical contributions to the listed program.
assessment.maturity: The ideas have endured across behavioral, labor, and organizational economics for decades.
uncertainties: External validity and context dependence of experimental social preferences remain active questions.
The literature includes several additional plausible contributors.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Law-and-finance research redirected attention to legal institutions, investor protection, and enforcement as determinants of financial development and corporate governance.
assessment.attribution: La Porta, Lopez-de-Silanes, and Shleifer were central coauthors of the foundational cross-country research program.
assessment.maturity: The work has had enduring influence across finance, development, and institutional economics.
uncertainties: Legal-origin interpretations and cross-country causal claims have faced substantial critique.
Measurement choices and institutional heterogeneity complicate general conclusions.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The reconstruction of long-run income and wealth inequality made distributional change and offshore wealth empirically tractable at unprecedented scale and public importance.
assessment.attribution: Piketty and Saez are central to the long-run inequality series, with Zucman a major contributor on wealth and offshore measurement.
assessment.maturity: The research has produced an extensive international data infrastructure and a large scholarly literature.
uncertainties: Top-income, wealth, and offshore-asset estimates require consequential assumptions and remain subject to revision.
The interpretation of descriptive inequality series for policy is contested.
